newsitem.title: FRANCE: France has record trade surplus, outlook improving.
newsitem.headline: France has record trade surplus, outlook improving.

text.p: The French government, fighting deep unpopularity, received welcome news on Tuesday as the October trade surplus posted a record high and a December industry survey showed the outlook continues to improve.

But the positive data, combined with a 25 percent gain on the Paris Bourse for the 1996 trading year and anecdotal evidence of a rush to the shops before Christmas, came against a background of a record 12.6 percent unemployment rate.

The customs office said on Tuesday that the seasonally adjusted trade surplus in October widened to 16.94 billion French franc ($3.23 billion) compared with a revised surplus in September of 9.70 billion franc.

More significantly, the surplus was not due to one-off factors such as exceptional sales of Airbus planes or defence exports. France accounted for 3.64 billion francs, or eight planes, in the October figure against 2.33 billion for six planes in September.
Defence exports were actually down 0.77 billion francs from 1.10 billion.
The higher surplus was the result of slowing imports and rising exports in industrial and agricultural products, while the franc's exchange rate remained stable.
Net exports to the rest of the European Union rose to 6.18 billion francs from 4.44 billion while the trade deficit with the United States was slashed to 1.11 billion francs from 2.57 billion francs.
The INSEE national statistics office, whose Paris building was damaged by a car bomb explosion on Monday night, said its industrial survey showed business leaders had become more optimistic.
"The general outlook for production is continuing to improve, even though the personal outlook is hardly changing and indicates moderate growth in the next three months," INSEE said in a statement.

"General price expectations are slightly recovering. Nevertheless, the personal price expectations are very depressed," it added, which means that businesses do not expect to be able to raise their prices.
An increase in production, a rise in demand and stable prices normally translates into higher economic growth. Both the government and the Bank of France have been making optimistic noises recently.
Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet told the Le Monde newspaper on Monday that economic growth would increase.
"We believe we have the capacity to do better in the medium term (than the 1.3 percent for 1996) -- 2.5 percent to three percent on average, per year, given the possible catch-up in growth," he said.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe said last week 1997 growth would at least double to a minimum 2.4 percent but employers' federation leader Jean Gandois judged that figure as too optimistic.
Bank of England governor Eddie George told the Le Figaro newspaper on Tuesday he was "perplexed" by calls for a higher dollar to boost European growth. He said the calls came essentially from France.
"Those who express it are also those who call for a drop in German interest rates. I don't think that these are appropriate remedies for Europe in an overall sense," George added.
